name: Leonardo da Vinci
teaser: Tuscan illegitimate son who was apprenticed at 14, sold almost nothing in life, died in 1519 at the French court — and his notebooks sold 1,800 years of scientific observation in 5,000 pages.

exploreAction.targetName: The Last Supper (Milan, restored) — sit on the opposite bench, separately
exploreAction.instruction: Sit where the original monks would have eaten. The composition is built around three windows and a strictly geometric 'Jesus at the center' rule, but the figures are so crammed with emotion that the geometry disappears on first viewing.

name: Michelangelo Buonarroti
teaser: Florentine sculptor who at 26 carved the marble David from a 17-foot block Carrara had already partly ruined. He painted the Sistine Chapel in four years while arguing with the Pope almost daily about money.

exploreAction.targetName: Sistine Chapel ceiling — visit between tour groups
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the separation of light and dark in the nine central panels. They're painted in fresco — water-based — onto wet plaster. Each day's painting had to complete a section. Michelangelo worked standing up, looking up, for years.

name: Raphael
teaser: Tuscan painter who died at 37 in 1520, leaving behind an enormous body of work that set the visual standard for the Italian Renaissance. The pope wept at his funeral.

exploreAction.targetName: The School of Athens (Stanza della Segnatura, Vatican)
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the central figures. Plato and Aristotle, the two founders of Western philosophy, walk with their hands extended: Plato toward the sky (idealism), Aristotle toward the ground (empiricism). Raphael was 25 when he painted this.

name: Caravaggio
teaser: Italian painter who fled Rome after killing a man in a tennis-game dispute, painted seven of his most important paintings while running from the law between Naples, Malta, and Sicily. He died at 39.

exploreAction.targetName: The Calling of St Matthew (Contarelli Chapel, Rome)
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the lighting. A single beam of light cuts across the room. Caravaggio didn't actually see this scene — he painted what an imagined harsh sunlight looked like on five men's backs. The painting technique is called 'tenebrism' — every shape emerges from...

name: Rembrandt van Rijn
teaser: Dutch painter who died bankrupt in 1669, painted almost 100 self-portraits, became the first artist whose drawings were sometimes valued more than his paintings (by connoisseurs, not by patrons).

exploreAction.targetName: The Night Watch (Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam)
exploreAction.instruction: Stand far first. Then close. Then return. The painting was cut on all four sides in 1715 to fit a wall — losing roughly 1m on each edge. Now the group doesn't look like a company on a mission; it looks like a wedding party.

name: Johannes Vermeer
teaser: Dutch painter who painted so slowly he produced 2-3 paintings a year, died at 43 leaving his wife and 11 children in debt. His work was largely forgotten for 200 years before being rediscovered in the 1860s.

exploreAction.targetName: Girl with a Pearl Earring (Mauritshuis, The Hague)
exploreAction.instruction: Look carefully at the pearl. Vermeer applied the highlight with a single thick stroke of white lead — slightly raised from the surface. Then look at the eye. The black is not simply painted — it's composed of two thin layers with different tinting.

name: Francisco Goya
teaser: Spanish court painter who recorded the Peninsular War and went deaf at 46 from an illness. His late work — the Black Paintings — were painted directly onto the walls of his house in the 14 years before he died.

exploreAction.targetName: The Third of May 1808 (Prado, Madrid)
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the man in the white shirt. He is about to be shot by a firing squad. The figure on the right is the lantern that lights him. The squareness of the lantern is what makes the man's shirt visible. The painting was completed 70 years before photography, and it's...

name: J. M. W. Turner
teaser: English painter who bequeathed 300 oil paintings and 30,000 drawings to the British Nation, trained himself on long canal-boat trips photographing the English light, and was so prolific the Tate has its own Turner Wing.

exploreAction.targetName: Snow Storm: Steam-Boat off a Harbour's Mouth (Tate)
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the painting for 5 minutes. The painting's blur is disqualifying to most modern viewers because it looks unfinished. It's actually a representation of a vision Turner had while lashed to a mast in a snowstorm in 1842.

name: John Constable
teaser: English painter who spent 30 years in his native Suffolk painting the same 6-square-mile stretch of river valley, sold almost no paintings in life, then revived as the founder of modern landscape painting.

exploreAction.targetName: The Hay Wain (National Gallery, London)
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the sky. Constable devoted more canvas to sky than to anything else. Heath-cloth pieces of cloud layered over a blue the color of a fresh-laundered shirt. He believed the English sky was the most painted-worthy object on Earth and rewrote European landscape...

name: Caspar David Friedrich
teaser: German Romantic painter who lost family members in horse-riding accidents as a child, then painted landscapes in which the figure always faces away from the viewer — looking out at the same sublime nature he did.

exploreAction.targetName: Wanderer above the Sea of Fog (Kunsthalle Hamburg)
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the figure. He's seen from behind. His hair is whipped by an unseen wind. He's looking out at fog over mountains. Friedrich believed the viewer's gaze should be directed by the painting. Look at the figure's posture — every muscle in the back is engaged.

name: Édouard Manet
teaser: French painter who exhibited Le Déjeuner sur l'herbe in 1863 and Le Olympia in 1865 — both paintings caused scandals by mixing classical pose with flat modern photographic light. He had been the leader of the Impressionists' teachers.

exploreAction.targetName: Olympia (Musée d'Orsay, Paris)
exploreAction.instruction: Look at Olympia. A young woman, fully nude, looks out at the viewer with confident composure. A black cat arches at her feet. A maid brings flowers. The painting caused a scandal in 1865 and still does. Manet used Titian's Venus of Urbino as a template and then...

name: Claude Monet
teaser: French painter who, by 1895, had painted 30 paintings of a single haystack. He refined the Impressionist formula until landscape became a controlled experiment in the perception of light.

exploreAction.targetName: Haystacks series at Musée d'Orsay or the National Gallery — view 3 of them side by side
exploreAction.instruction: Look at three paintings at once. Each haystack is the same subject, painted within months of each other. The sun is in different positions. He showed you what changes when light changes. That's the entire case for Impressionism in three paintings.

name: Paul Cézanne
teaser: French painter who wrote his mother from Paris that he was starving but unable to bring himself to paint for money. His work became the foundation of Cubism.

exploreAction.targetName: Mont Sainte-Victoire paintings (one at the Tate, one at the Met) — view as a pair
exploreAction.instruction: Look at two paintings of the same mountain side by side. Cézanne painted 60 of them. Each one is a different conceptualization of how 3D form sits in 2D space. Picasso said Cézanne was 'the father of us all' — Cubism starts here.

name: Vincent van Gogh
teaser: Dutch painter who sold one painting in life (The Red Vineyard), wrote his brother Theo 800 letters over 21 years — and within 18 months of his suicide, became a household name in Europe.

exploreAction.targetName: The Starry Night (MoMA, New York)
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the brushstroke pattern. Each star is a slightly different spiral. Each cloud moves differently. Van Gogh's thick brushstroke technique, called impasto, is what makes each element physical. Now look at the cypress tree — it's painted from the bottom up, like a...

name: Paul Gauguin
teaser: French banker turned painter, stockbroker at 35, abandoned his family for Brittany, then Tahiti, where he painted his most famous canvases while drinking absinthe and arguing with the local Catholic mission.

exploreAction.targetName: Where Do We Come From? What Are We? Where Are We Going? (Tate)
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the painting's three sections. Gauguin painted the whole thing in two weeks, intended it to be his last work, and tried to poison himself afterward. Read right-to-left (he's Polynesian at the right, dying at the left).

name: Berthe Morisot
teaser: French painter who exhibited in 7 of the 8 Impressionist exhibitions between 1874 and 1886 — more than any other artist. She died at 54, then her daughter published her correspondence with Mallarmé.

exploreAction.targetName: Woman at Her Toilette (Art Institute of Chicago)
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the brushwork. Morisot paints with almost transparent washes and an almost-blank background. Her eye was trained to look at how figures absorb light; she said she never tried to finish a painting. Instead she caught figures mid-gesture.

name: Mary Cassatt
teaser: American painter who left Philadelphia for Paris at 23, became Edgar Degas's only American student, exhibited in 4 Impressionist shows, painted children and women in ways Impressionism had not.

exploreAction.targetName: The Child's Bath (Art Institute of Chicago)
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the hands. Cassatt's hands — the mother's on her daughter's shoulder, the daughter's small feet at the basin — are painted with what feels like a printer's precision. This is a painting of mother and daughter in an ordinary moment.

name: Pablo Picasso
teaser: Spanish painter who at 17 drew with a precision that took the Spanish crown 19 years to believe was a real painting. He invented Cubism at 25 with Braque and kept painting until the day he died at 91.

exploreAction.targetName: Les Demoiselles d'Avignon (MoMA)
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the women's faces. The two on the right have masks painted in African-style angular forms. Picasso saw the African masks at the Musée d'Ethnographie du Trocadéro in 1907 and the painting changed that year. Two years later he and Braque would found Cubism.

name: Henri Matisse
teaser: French painter whose Fauvist debut (1905) showed canvases of clashing pure color — a critic called it 'les fauves' (the wild beasts). His late cut-paper works, made in his 80s while bed-bound, are his most famous.

exploreAction.targetName: The Snail (Tate Modern)
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the composition. The painting is painted on a 9-foot square of paper cut into 49 pieces — Matisse glued the pieces back onto the canvas with the colors in reverse. He made it in bed after surgery. The painting is about a snail's spiral.

name: Wassily Kandinsky
teaser: Russian painter who heard painting as music, kept a notebook mapping colors to specific musical instruments, abandoned figurative painting for pure abstraction and founded the Bauhaus color theory course.

exploreAction.targetName: Composition VIII (Guggenheim)
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the colors as sound. Kandinsky mapped yellow to trumpets, blue to cellos, and orange to sustained middle-register blasts. The geometry in this painting is impossible without sound. Look at the largest yellow shape — does it actually make your chest expand?

name: Piet Mondrian
teaser: Dutch painter who moved to NYC in 1940 after London because NYC's skyscrapers looked to him like Braque's drawings. He died four years later, having painted his last canvases to the sound of boogie-woogie.

exploreAction.targetName: Composition with Red, Blue, and Yellow (Guggenheim)
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the white lines. Most of the painting is white. The black lines divide the canvas into uneven squares, three of which contain a single pure color: red, blue, yellow. Mondrian spent 30 years narrowing his vocabulary to this.

name: Jackson Pollock
teaser: American painter who's said to have invented 'action painting' — laying a canvas on the floor and flinging paint at it with sticks and brushes. His 1949 painting Number 1A was bought 30 years later for $58M.

exploreAction.targetName: One: Number 31, 1950 (MoMA) — view from a distance
exploreAction.instruction: Stand back first. Then walk in. Pollock's paintings are non-compositional — they work as physical record of a body's movement. He laid the canvas on the floor and walked around it, flinging paint from a stick. Look for the moments where the drip ran — they're the...

name: Mark Rothko
teaser: Latvian-American painter who painted in pairs of rectangles that simply float over a monochrome ground — and committed suicide at 66 in 1970 after completing the Rothko Chapel in Houston.

exploreAction.targetName: Rothko Chapel (Houston) — sit in silence for 30 min
exploreAction.instruction: Sit. Don't read. Don't look at your phone. The Rothko Chapel holds 14 paintings in an octagonal room. Sit on the bench in front of any one of them. The painter's intent was that the painting would be the room's atmosphere, not an object.

name: Andy Warhol
teaser: Pittsburgh commercial artist who invented the silkscreen-multiple and the celebrity-as-product. He ran the Factory as a yearlong continuous performance that became the most influential art space of the 1960s.

exploreAction.targetName: Marilyn Diptych (Tate Modern) — get in close
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the second canvas. The silkscreen's imperfections are visible: ink-skip, register offset, smudged edges. Warhol never retouched them. He said he wanted the gold Marilyn to be the side you stare at and the black Marilyn to be the side that stares back.

name: David Hockney
teaser: British painter who at 26 painted A Bigger Splash, became the first artist to send a video overtly fishing for men, and at 71 turned to digital painting on his iPad — making it the most-listened-to tool of his career.

exploreAction.targetName: A Bigger Splash (Tate)
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the painting. Two weeks, no figures, just a swimming pool and an inland LA house. He painted the splash itself in 9 seconds and then spent a week analyzing the spray pattern. Look at the splash distorting the water — the splash is the painting.

name: Georgia O'Keeffe
teaser: American painter who at the New York galleries of the 1920s taught Americans that flowers can be more than decoration and bones more than reminder — and persisted in her work past age 90.

exploreAction.targetName: Cow's Skull with Calico Roses (Art Institute of Chicago)
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the painting. A bleached white cow skull with red roses behind it. O'Keeffe said she painted it because 'Texas is a state with nothing in it.' Now look at the painting's relation to scale — the skull fills the frame.

name: Frida Kahlo
teaser: Mexican painter who dressed in Tehuana costume, painted almost exclusively self-portraits because she spent 30 years ill in a body cast after a bus crash, and died in 1954 at 47 with a final diary page: 'I hope the exit is joyful — and I hope never to come back.'

exploreAction.targetName: The Two Fridas (Museo de Arte Moderno, Mexico City)
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the two figures. Frida painted two versions of herself sitting side by side after her divorce from Diego Rivera. One wears European dress, one wears Tehuana costume. Their hands are linked by a shared vein.

name: Katsushika Hokusai
teaser: Japanese ukiyo-e woodblock printmaker who created The Great Wave off Kanagawa at 70, drew 30,000 prints in 70 years, and spent most of his life saying he hadn't yet learned to draw.

exploreAction.targetName: The Great Wave off Kanagawa (any of the 30+ surviving impressions)
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the wave. The fingers of foam are not waves — they're claws. Behind the wave, Mount Fuji sits still. The composition balances motion (the wave) against stillness (Fuji). The blue is prussian blue, imported.

name: Utagawa Hiroshige
teaser: Japanese ukiyo-e artist of the 100 Famous Views of Edo series, whose prints influenced European Impressionists a half-century later. Van Gogh copied two of them.

exploreAction.targetName: Sudden Shower over Shin-Ōhashi Bridge (Met Museum)
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the rain. Hiroshige bridged the rain by slashing diagonal lines across the print. The figures lean with their bodies to hold their hats. Van Gogh copied this in oil and donated the copy to his brother. Look at the leftmost figure, half-turning, holding his hat...

name: Ai Weiwei
teaser: Chinese conceptual artist and activist whose studio designed the Beijing National Stadium, was arrested and detained 81 days in 2011 for tax evasion after criticizing the state.

exploreAction.targetName: Sunflower Seeds at Tate Modern — look from above
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the installation as a whole, then walk to the front and inspect one seed. The installation is 100M hand-painted porcelain sunflower seeds. Several years and 1,600 artisans. Each seed was sculpted and hand-painted identically.

name: Banksy
teaser: Anonymous British street artist whose identity is unknown even to most art-market insiders. His 2018 'Girl with Balloon' self-shredded at Sotheby's right after being sold for $1.4M.

exploreAction.targetName: Any permanently-installed Banksy work — see the Banksy vs. Bristol Museum page for live street locations in Bristol / NYC / Bethlehem
exploreAction.instruction: Don't go looking for a specific image. The best Banksy hits are ambient: a rat stenciled to a wall, a child chasing an imaginary friend. Look at the placement — Banksy always chooses a site that adds meaning to the image. See if you can find five within a 2-mile walk.

name: Louise Bourgeois
teaser: French-American sculptor who worked in her NY studio from the 1940s until she died at 98 in 2010. She invented the first 'Spider' (Maman) at 80 — 30 feet tall, now sited in cities around the world.

exploreAction.targetName: Maman (any major-city version: 21st Century Tate, Bilbao Guggenheim, São Paulo, Doha, etc.)
exploreAction.instruction: Walk under the spider. Bourgeois said the sculpture was a tribute to her mother — a textile restorer who held the family together through her father's affairs. Walk counter-clockwise around the legs. Look at the marble eggs in the body of the spider.

name: Constantin Brancusi
teaser: Romanian sculptor who lived in Paris for 50 years, refused to make exhibitions of his sculptures in his lifetime because they lost meaning without his own installation, left the Romanian government an enormous body of work.

exploreAction.targetName: Bird in Space (any one — at the Met, MoMA, Tate) — sit and look for 15 min
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the sculpture. It's a tall sliver of polished bronze. In 1926, the US courts ruled that Bird in Space was NOT an artwork for tax purposes — because it didn't look like a bird. Brancusi's point is that you should feel its flight, not look for its beak.

name: Auguste Rodin
teaser: French sculptor whose 1904 'Balzac' was rejected as 'a sack of coal' by the Société des Gens de Lettres but became the first modern sculpture; his 1889 Burghers of Calais sits as a public sculpture in front of city halls worldwide.

exploreAction.targetName: The Burghers of Calais (any of 12 castings — Hôtel de Ville in Calais, Victoria Tower Gardens in London, Hirshhorn in DC)
exploreAction.instruction: Walk around the sculpture. Rodin placed the figures at ground level — no pedestal. Walk the perimeter slowly. Each burgher is a specific historical person walking to his death. You should feel that the figures are as tall as you are.

name: Ansel Adams
teaser: American photographer who at 14 taught himself a piano technique on a damaged piano, then made the Yosemite landscape a national concern by photographing it in his own 70-year-old camera.

exploreAction.targetName: Moonrise, Hernandez, New Mexico (any print at SFMOMA, MFA Boston, or Met)
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the clouds. Adams shot this negative at 5 p.m. in 1941 in negative light. The exposure was 1 second at f/8. He developed the print in his 'Zone System' — dividing the world into 10 stops of dark/light. Notice the moon's position — the negative's reverse side.

name: Dorothea Lange
teaser: American documentary photographer whose Migrant Mother (1936) became the most recognized photograph of the Great Depression. The woman in the photo (Florence Owens Thompson) didn't know her image had been published until 30 years later.

exploreAction.targetName: Migrant Mother (MoMA, prints 001–007)
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the woman's eyes. Her hands are around the youngest child — they have nothing left but their weight. Lange asked her to take the children out of focus — 'without names, the children could be any of the migrant children.

name: Robert Frank
teaser: Swiss-American photographer whose 1958 book The Americans changed American documentary photography in a single volume. Jack Kerouac wrote the introduction in three hours.

exploreAction.targetName: The Americans (whole book — public library or any museum copy)
exploreAction.instruction: Read the book in one sitting. Frank shot 27,000 frames over two years; he chose 83 for the book. Each photograph is an indictment, observation, or joke. Look at frame 24 (Charleston, SC) — a Black man with a white child on his shoulders — then frame 25 (a passenger...

name: Diane Arbus
teaser: American photographer who, between 1962 and 1971, found 230 of the most otherized people in American suburbia and photographed them, then killed herself at 48. 'A photograph is a secret about a secret.'

exploreAction.targetName: Identical Twins, Roselle, New Jersey (MoMA or Met)
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the twins — they were 7 years old. They're not identical at this age; the photograph catches a moment of unconscious mirroring. Arbus insisted on using a square format, and the Rolleiflex TLR was heavy enough to slow her down.

name: Cindy Sherman
teaser: American photographer who appears as every character in every one of her photographs — never as herself. Her Untitled Film Stills (1977–80) became the most important photo series of the late 20th century.

exploreAction.targetName: Untitled Film Stills (MoMA or any museum collection — at least 10 prints)
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the prints as a sequence. Sherman never appears in her own photographs as Cindy Sherman — she is always a character. The most-cited single image is #6 (crop top + sunglasses + sidewalk). Look at the way she uses lighting to imply films you've never seen — the...

name: Yoko Ono
teaser: Japanese-American artist whose 1964 book Grapefruit read as a Fluxus score, collaborated with John Lennon, and prefigured conceptual art 5+ years before it became a movement.

exploreAction.targetName: Read Yoko Ono's "Grapefruit" — pick 3 instructions at random and complete them
exploreAction.instruction: Pick any three instructions. Examples: 'Imagine the clouds dripping. Dig a hole in your garden to fit your size.' 'Listen to the sound of the Earth turning.' Do them slowly. Ono's instructions are the artist's 'Work' — the canvas is the audience's act.

name: Gustav Klimt
teaser: The leader of the Vienna Secession scandalized Austrian society by painting sex — the university ceiling commissions were so controversial the faculty refused to hang them. His 'golden phase' — The Kiss, Adele Bloch-Bauer I — is the most reproduced image of the era, and the Bloch-Bauer portrait's legal history (looted by Nazis, recovered, sold for $135 million) made him a courtroom figure a century after his death.

exploreAction.targetName: Gustav Klimt — 'The Kiss' (1908) and the university ceiling paintings
exploreAction.instruction: Look at The Kiss and then at the university ceiling paintings (Philosophy, Medicine, Jurisprudence) side by side: one is velvet decoration, the other is a war on convention. Then find the 'Golden Adele' and read its provenance — the 2006 restitution case that rewrote the rules for Nazi-looted art. Klimt's bodies are made of ornament; the question is whether the ornament hides them or IS them.

name: Edvard Munch
teaser: Munch's The Scream — painted in 1893 — is the second-most-famous image in Western art after the Mona Lisa, and he made four versions of it. He wrote the moment down first: 'I felt the great scream throughout nature,' after a sunset turned 'blood red' — and he described his art as a diary of 'the modern life of the soul.'

exploreAction.targetName: Edvard Munch — 'The Scream' (1893) and 'The Sun' (1911)
exploreAction.instruction: Read Munch's diary entry about the sunset, then look at the 1893 version in Oslo's National Museum: the screaming figure has no ears, and the landscape is doing the screaming. Then look at 'The Sun' (1911), painted twenty years later — the same artist who made the scream painted a blazing, joyful sunrise for Oslo University's hall; the difference is the whole story of his career.

name: Marc Chagall
teaser: Chagall painted flying lovers, fiddlers, and upside-down villages — the folk world of his Jewish childhood in Vitebsk lifted into the air. He was a pioneer of modernism who refused to join any modern movement, and he also designed the stained-glass windows of Jerusalem's Hadassah hospital and the ceiling of the Paris Opera.

exploreAction.targetName: Marc Chagall — 'I and the Village' (1911) and the Paris Opera ceiling
exploreAction.instruction: Look at 'I and the Village' (1911) and trace the non-Euclidean space: the cow's head, the man's face, the village — all sharing one canvas without perspective. Then find the Paris Opera ceiling (1964), which he painted at 77, suspended over the audience — Chagall's answer to the question of how a folk painter survives modernism: he took his village with him wherever he went.

name: Salvador Dalí
teaser: Dalí painted the most famous surrealist image ever made — The Persistence of Memory (1931), with its melting watches — and turned surrealism into performance art before the term existed: the anteater, the mustache, the submarine press conferences. He claimed his method, 'paranoia-criticism,' let him see images in the world that weren't there.

exploreAction.targetName: Salvador Dalí — 'The Persistence of Memory' (1931) and the Civil War painting
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the melting watches and then read Dalí's own explanation: he said they were 'the camembert cheese of time' — he'd been eating soft cheese before a dream. Then find 'Soft Construction with Boiled Beans (Premonition of Civil War)' (1936): the same painter who made the soft watches painted a screaming self-dismembering figure a few years later, and it is not a joke. Compare the two and decide what Dalí was really after.

name: Paul Klee
teaser: Klee — who described drawing as 'taking a line for a walk' — was a Swiss-German artist who taught at the Bauhaus and made over 9,000 works in small, jewel-like formats. His Twittering Machine (1922) is one of the most beloved and unsettling images of the century: a machine that may be birds, or may be a torture device, drawn with four squiggles.

exploreAction.targetName: Paul Klee — 'Twittering Machine' (1922) and the 'Creative Credo'
exploreAction.instruction: Look at 'Twittering Machine' and count what's actually there: a crank, four birds, a wire — nothing else, and it still reads as a horror scene. Then read Klee's 1920 'Creative Credo,' where he wrote that art 'does not reproduce the visible; it makes visible.' The tiny scale of most Klees is deliberate — he said the small format forces the viewer to come close, which is where the work happens.

name: Diego Rivera
teaser: Rivera painted the 20th century's most ambitious public murals — the 27 panels of the Detroit Industry cycle and the Rockefeller Center commission that was destroyed when he refused to remove a portrait of Lenin. He is also remembered for his marriage to Frida Kahlo, which was as much an artwork as any mural.

exploreAction.targetName: Diego Rivera — 'Detroit Industry' (1933) and the Rockefeller Center story
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the Detroit Industry murals and notice the politics inside the machinery: Rivera painted assembly lines as cathedrals, with workers as the congregation — and then put a child being born among the gears. Then read the Rockefeller Center story: he painted 'Man at the Crossroads,' the Rockefellers had it chipped off the wall in 1934, and Rivera re-created it in Mexico City as 'Man, Controller of the Universe.'

name: Edward Hopper
teaser: Hopper's Nighthawks (1942) — four people in a diner at night, none talking — is the iconic image of American urban loneliness, and Hopper himself said he was 'unconsciously painting the loneliness of a large city.' He painted it shortly after Pearl Harbor, during the blackouts, when windows were darkened — which may be why the diner glows so hard.

exploreAction.targetName: Edward Hopper — 'Nighthawks' (1942) and 'Early Sunday Morning'
exploreAction.instruction: Look at Nighthawks and notice what's missing: no door visible to the street, a counter that ends where the window begins, and the four figures separated by exactly the width of the countertop. Then look at 'Early Sunday Morning' (1930), the empty street Hopper painted a decade before — the loneliness was there before the war. Hopper's wife Jo modeled all the women in his paintings, which adds a strange self-portrait layer to every one.

name: Norman Rockwell
teaser: Rockwell painted 322 Saturday Evening Post covers over 47 years, making him the most reproduced artist in American history — and he was dismissed as an illustrator until late in life, when critics began arguing the best of his work is genuine art. His 1964 painting of Ruby Bridges, a six-year-old Black girl walking to school past a wall scrawled with a racial slur, is now among the most important images of the civil rights era.

exploreAction.targetName: Norman Rockwell — 'The Problem We All Live With' (1964)
exploreAction.instruction: Look at 'The Problem We All Live With' (1964) and notice the details Rockwell chose: the tomato splatter, the marshals' badges, the white dresses of the guards' presence — and the girl's dignity. Then read the history: Rockwell left the Post the year before over censorship (the Post refused to run an anti-segregation image), and this painting appeared in Look magazine instead.

name: Francis Bacon
teaser: Bacon's screaming, distorted figures — most famously his 1953 reworking of Velázquez's portrait of Pope Innocent X — are among the most violent images in modern painting. He worked from photographs, never from life, and once said of the pope series: 'I wanted to paint the scream more than the horror... I feel ever so sorry for the Pope but I have no choice.'

exploreAction.targetName: Francis Bacon — 'Study after Velázquez' (1953) vs. the Velázquez original
exploreAction.instruction: Look at Velázquez's original portrait of Innocent X (1650) and then Bacon's 'Study after Velázquez's Portrait of Pope Innocent X' (1953) side by side: same pose, different universe. Then read what Bacon kept and broke — the purple drapery, the gilded chair survive; the face dissolves into screaming strokes. Bacon claimed the distortion made the image more real, and the comparison is the test of that claim.

name: Bridget Riley
teaser: Riley's black-and-white paintings of the mid-1960s — precise stripes and curves that appear to move, shimmer, and bulge — made her the leading figure of Op Art and the first woman to win the International Prize at the Venice Biennale (1968). She insisted the movement was in the viewer's eye, not the canvas.

exploreAction.targetName: Bridget Riley — 'Movement in Squares' (1961) and the Venice win
exploreAction.instruction: Look at 'Movement in Squares' (1961) and let your eye move across it slowly: the squares contract, bow, and spring back — entirely on the flat canvas. Then read Riley's claim about her intent: she said she was trying to 'make visible the tensions and energies that we feel but cannot name,' and that the optical effects were a means, not an end. Her later work dropped black-and-white for color, which changes everything.

name: Anselm Kiefer
teaser: Kiefer, born in Germany in 1945 — the year the war ended — has spent his career confronting what German artists after the war preferred to forget: his early photographs show him giving the Nazi salute in landscapes, and his paintings are built from ash, straw, lead, and charred books. He is the most important artist to take the Holocaust as his explicit subject.

exploreAction.targetName: Anselm Kiefer — 'Your Golden Hair, Margarete' (1981) and the lead books
exploreAction.instruction: Look at 'Your Golden Hair, Margarete' (1981) — the poem by Paul Celan about a Jewish woman and a German woman, made visible as straw and ash — and then at Kiefer's lead books, which weigh more than a person and are displayed like reliquaries. The materials matter: ash is memory, lead is history's weight, and Kiefer's scale makes the viewer small inside it.

name: Yayoi Kusama
teaser: Kusama has painted dots since childhood — she saw them in hallucinations and believed they were her way to 'obliterate' the world — and she voluntarily moved into a psychiatric hospital in Tokyo in 1977, where she still lives and works. Her Infinity Mirror Rooms, begun in the 1960s and revived in the 2010s, have become the most-photographed artworks on Earth.

exploreAction.targetName: Yayoi Kusama — 'Infinity Nets' (1958) and the pumpkins
exploreAction.instruction: Read Kusama's own account of her hallucinations — she wrote that she began making dots 'as a result of the pathology' — then look at 'Infinity Nets' (1958), painted in New York when she was inventing a radical alternative to abstract expressionism. Then find the polka-dot pumpkin she returns to constantly: she has said the pumpkin is her 'alter ego,' and its comforting shape is the exact opposite of the obliterating dots.

name: Yoshitomo Nara
teaser: Nara's paintings of sullen, big-headed children — girls with knives, cigarettes, or simply flat stares — made him the face of Japanese neo-pop and, in 2019, one of the most expensive living Asian artists when one sold for $25 million. He has said the children are not cute but 'the unknown soldier of the void.'

exploreAction.targetName: Yoshitomo Nara — 'Knife Behind Back' (2000) and the neo-pop children
exploreAction.instruction: Look at 'Knife Behind Back' (2000) and read the expression carefully: the girl is not angry so much as armored, and the painting's title does the work the face won't. Then read Nara's method: he works from memories of his own isolated childhood in postwar Japan, and the children are never victims — they're survivors. The scale shift matters too: his small paintings feel like secrets, his large ones like accusations.

name: Lee Krasner
teaser: Krasner was a major abstract expressionist who spent most of her career known as 'Mrs. Jackson Pollock' — the marriage eclipsing the work. Her 'Little Image' series of the late 1940s, dense all-over paintings built from tiny marks, anticipated the style Pollock became famous for, and after his death she emerged as one of the most rigorous painters of her generation.

exploreAction.targetName: Lee Krasner — 'Little Image' series (1946–49) and the postwar collages
exploreAction.instruction: Look at a 'Little Image' painting (1946–49) and notice the scale: some are under two feet, built from thousands of small strokes in grids and spirals — made before Pollock's drip paintings. Then read the art-historical problem: how much of Pollock's all-over style grew out of watching Krasner work? The scholarship is careful, but the timeline is public.

name: Agnes Martin
teaser: Martin's paintings — grids, horizontal bands, and delicate lines on six-foot square canvases — look like minimalism but were made as a form of devotion: she called them her 'response to the beauty of the world.' She abandoned painting for eight years in the late 1960s, drove across the country, and returned with the grids that made her famous.

exploreAction.targetName: Agnes Martin — the grid paintings (1960s) and 'The Islands' (1999)
exploreAction.instruction: Look at a Martin grid and read her own description of what it is: she said her paintings 'have neither objects, nor space, nor time, nor anything — no forms' — and that she wanted to express 'the abstract response to nature' the way music does. Then read her biography: she was diagnosed with schizophrenia, and she painted the serenity on the other side of the illness.

name: Alice Neel
teaser: Neel painted portraits for 60 years and called herself 'a collector of souls' — her sitters, from neighbors to Andy Warhol to the pregnant Linda Nochlin, are rendered with unsparing honesty and electric color. She was virtually unknown until the 1970s, when the feminist art movement rediscovered her; her portrait of Warhol, showing his surgery scars, is one of the century's great images.

exploreAction.targetName: Alice Neel — 'Andy Warhol' (1970) and the 80-year-old self-portrait
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the Warhol portrait (1970) — painted months after Valerie Solanas shot him, Neel shows the scars and the corset — and notice how she refuses flattery while staying tender. Then read her method: she said she painted 'the person, not the pose,' and that she tried to catch 'the absolute reality.' Compare her self-portrait at 80 (1980), naked and unflinching, with any portrait by her male peers: the honesty is the style.

name: Betye Saar
teaser: Saar's assemblages — boxes and collages built from found objects, racist memorabilia, and spiritual imagery — turned the African American domestic and sacred into high art. Her 1972 work 'The Liberation of Aunt Jemima,' which arms the mammy figure with a rifle and a fist, is one of the most important artworks of the Black Power era.

exploreAction.targetName: Betye Saar — 'The Liberation of Aunt Jemima' (1972) and 'The Black Girl's Window'
exploreAction.instruction: Look at 'The Liberation of Aunt Jemima' (1972) and unpack the layers: the mammy figurine inside a box, the Aunt Jemima product label, the grenade in one hand and the rifle in the other. Then read Saar's account of finding the figurine and deciding to 'liberate' her. Her later work — 'The Black Girl's Window' (1969) is the masterpiece — folds astrology, mysticism, and memory into the same boxes.

name: Lorna Simpson
teaser: Simpson's photographs of the 1980s and 90s — often of Black women seen from behind, paired with text — were among the first artworks to use photography to deconstruct how Black identity is looked at. 'Guarded Conditions' (1989), with its repeated images and ambiguous captions, made her, in 1990, the first Black woman to show at the Venice Biennale's main exhibition.

exploreAction.targetName: Lorna Simpson — 'Guarded Conditions' (1989) and the 'Snow' series
exploreAction.instruction: Look at 'Guarded Conditions' and read the words: 'sex attacks, skin attacks' — the caption system is the work. Then read why Simpson photographs her subjects from behind: she has said the back view denies the viewer the 'read' they expect, forcing attention to the frame, the text, and the systems that shape how Black women are seen.

name: Kehinde Wiley
teaser: Wiley paints Black people in the grand poses and settings of European portraiture — his street-cast subjects sit astride rearing horses or against ornate wallpaper — and in 2018 he painted the official portrait of Barack Obama, the first African American president's portrait by an African American artist. The portraits ask who gets to be painted like royalty.

exploreAction.targetName: Kehinde Wiley — 'Napoleon Leading the Army over the Alps' (2005) and the Obama portrait
exploreAction.instruction: Look at 'Napoleon Leading the Army over the Alps' (2005) — a young Black man in sneakers on a rearing horse, replacing Jacques-Louis David's Napoleon — and notice what Wiley keeps: the pose, the drama, the heroism. Then read his casting method: he approaches strangers on the street and invites them to sit for paintings that cost more than a house. The Obama portrait is the same logic at the highest stakes.

name: Toyin Ojih Odutola
teaser: Odutola draws with ballpoint pens — thousands of dense, deliberate marks that build skin, fabric, and landscape — and her subjects are often imagined: entire fictional aristocratic Nigerian families rendered in ballpoint on paper. She has said she is interested in 'the politics of mark-making,' and her drawings take months each.

exploreAction.targetName: Toyin Ojih Odutola — the ballpoint portraits and 'A Countervailing Theory'
exploreAction.instruction: Look at a close-up of her ballpoint technique: the skin is built from layered hatch marks in black, blue, and red ink, each stroke deliberate. Then read her 2017 'A Countervailing Theory' series, which imagines two fictional Nigerian families across generations — the drawings are a novel told in portraiture, and the imagined status of the subjects is the point: she draws what representation could look like.

name: Mickalene Thomas
teaser: Thomas makes enormous portraits of Black women — often her mother, always from life — covered in rhinestones, patterned fabrics, and household interiors straight out of 1970s Black living rooms. Her 'Le Déjeuner sur l'herbe: Les trois femmes noires' (2010) re-stages Manet's picnic with Black women in full ownership of the frame.

exploreAction.targetName: Mickalene Thomas — 'Le Déjeuner sur l'herbe: Les trois femmes noires' (2010)
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the rhinestones up close: Thomas sets them one by one into the paint, so the work changes from a distance (portrait) to close (glittering surface). Then compare her 'Le Déjeuner sur l'herbe' with Manet's original: same composition, opposite politics — Manet's nude is objectified, Thomas's women are in charge. The materials — rhinestones, wood veneer, enamel — are the language of Black domestic aesthetics she grew up with.

name: Julie Mehretu
teaser: Mehretu builds paintings at architectural scale from thousands of layered marks — architectural drawings, maps, calligraphy, and abstract gestures — that read like exploded cities seen from orbit. Her work asks what history looks like as form: she has said she wants to 'make a space for the imagination to move in.'

exploreAction.targetName: Julie Mehretu — 'Grey Area' (2009) and the layered cities
exploreAction.instruction: Look at a large Mehretu ('Grey Area' is the gateway) and spend time separating the layers: the base is an architectural plan, the middle is drawn maps and notations, the top is gestural strokes that erase and puncture what's below.

name: Tschabalala Self
teaser: Self builds Black female bodies from stitched fabric, paint, and print — her figures are part sculpture, part painting, and they inhabit the space of Harlem bodegas, bedrooms, and streets. Her series 'Bodega Run' (2016) turned the corner store into a stage, and her layered technique makes the body itself read as assembled rather than given.

exploreAction.targetName: Tschabalala Self — 'Bodega Run' (2016) and the fabric-painted figures
exploreAction.instruction: Look at 'Bodega Run' and notice how the figures are made: the skin is fabric sewn into the canvas, the hair is yarn, the pose is painted over the cloth — Self has said she wants to 'represent the black female body as a site of complexity.' Then read her stated project: the bodies are never passive objects of looking; they're occupied, active, and built, and the seams are deliberately visible.

name: Flora Yukhnovich
teaser: Yukhnovich paints rococo — the frothy 18th-century style of Tiepolo and Boucher — as seen through a modern lens: her canvases of billowing fabric, clouds, and naked nymphs dissolve into abstract brushwork, and she has said she is 're-presenting' historical painting 'through the filter of how we see images now.'

exploreAction.targetName: Flora Yukhnovich — 'If I Were a Melon' (2018) and the rococo sources
exploreAction.instruction: Look at 'If I Were a Melon' (2018) and then at the Tiepolo it descends from: Yukhnovich keeps the rococo's swelling forms but removes the story, so the composition becomes pure movement. Then read her process: she begins with found images — including low-resolution internet reproductions — and the soft-focus, filtered look of her surfaces is deliberate, not accidental. She is painting what the 18th century looks like after Instagram.

name: Shara Hughes
teaser: Hughes paints invented landscapes — vivid, imaginary views that borrow from salt marshes, coastlines, and the pattern of a tulip poplar, but exist nowhere on Earth. She has said her landscapes are 'portraits' of places she's never been, and her work broke out in the 2010s as a rare fusion of landscape painting and contemporary abstraction.

exploreAction.targetName: Shara Hughes — the invented landscapes and the salt-marsh series
exploreAction.instruction: Look at a Hughes landscape and notice the tension: the forms suggest a real place (a marsh, a ridge) while the color and brushwork refuse to confirm it. Then read her method: she works from memory, imagination, and close observation of natural light, painting the feeling of a place rather than its coordinates.

name: Otis Kwame Kye Quaicoe
teaser: Quaicoe, a Ghanaian painter, makes large portraits of Black men and women whose presence fills the canvas — subjects in sharp suits, sunglasses, and confident poses against flat, graphic backgrounds. He has said he paints 'the self-assuredness of the people around me,' and his work became a market sensation in the early 2020s.

exploreAction.targetName: Otis Kwame Kye Quaicoe — the 'self-assured' portraits of Black men
exploreAction.instruction: Look at a Quaicoe portrait and read the pose: the figures meet the viewer's gaze with an ease that borders on challenge, and the flat monochrome backgrounds push the figure forward. Then read the context of his breakthrough: he trained in Ghana, moved to the US, and his portraits of 'men on the move' — musicians, boxers, neighbors — made him, by 2021, one of the most collected living African artists.

name: Issy Wood
teaser: Wood paints deadpan images of ordinary things — cars, teeth, silk dresses, a single chair — sourced from screenshots and catalogues, in a muted palette that makes the everyday feel ominous. She also makes music under the name 'Sega Bodega' collaborators, and her paintings' flatness is a statement about how images circulate now.

exploreAction.targetName: Issy Wood — the deadpan object paintings and the screenshot method
exploreAction.instruction: Look at a Wood painting of an everyday object (a car interior, a dress on a hanger) and notice the tone: the image is rendered with perfect competence and no emotion, which is precisely the point. Then read her method: she works from photographs she collects — including screenshots, catalogues, and her own camera roll — and the paintings' deadpan surface is a critique of how images carry feeling (or fail to).

name: Caroline Walker
teaser: Walker paints women in domestic and workplace interiors — hotel maids, cleaners, office workers, women at home — with a cool, observational realism. She has said she is interested in 'the gap between the way women are seen and the way they see themselves,' and her paintings are built from photographs of staged scenes.

exploreAction.targetName: Caroline Walker — the women-at-work paintings and the staged-photo method

name: Fra Angelico
teaser: Fra Angelico — 'the angelic brother' — was a Dominican friar who painted the frescoes of San Marco in Florence, where his own order lived, in the 1430s–40s. Every cell of the monastery's upper floor has one fresco, designed to be prayed in front of; he was beatified by the Catholic Church in 1982, making him possibly the only painter ever formally declared blessed.

exploreAction.targetName: Fra Angelico — the San Marco 'Annunciation' (c. 1440)
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the San Marco 'Annunciation' — painted in the corridor where the friars walked — and notice the architecture: the loggia frames the moment so that the viewer stands where the friar stood, in the space the angel and Mary share. Then compare it with his 'Annunciation' in Cortona, made for a different audience: same subject, different geometry, because Fra Angelico painted for the room, not the museum.

name: Hieronymus Bosch
teaser: Bosch painted the strangest images of the Renaissance — the Garden of Earthly Delights (c. 1500) teems with hybrid creatures, giant fruit, and rituals that scholars still argue about, 500 years later. He worked in 's-Hertogenbosch, never left, and his exact theological intent remains the most contested question in the history of art.

exploreAction.targetName: Hieronymus Bosch — 'The Garden of Earthly Delights' (c. 1500), central panel
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the Garden of Earthly Delights' central panel and try to find a single 'normal' human action — the nudity, the giant strawberries, the glass spheres, the owls — and then read the main interpretations: it is either a warning against lust, a celebration of earthly paradise before the Fall, or an alchemical allegory. Then look at the right panel, Hell, where a pair of ears holds a knife: nobody has ever fully explained that, either.

name: Albrecht Dürer
teaser: Dürer was the first artist to paint himself as Christ, the first to make self-portraits as a deliberate series, and the printmaker whose woodcuts and engravings — the Rhinoceros, Melencolia I — defined what 'a master print' means. He was also the first German artist to be famous in Italy, where he traveled twice to study the new Renaissance ideas.

exploreAction.targetName: Albrecht Dürer — 'Melencolia I' (1514) and the 1500 self-portrait
exploreAction.instruction: Look at 'Melencolia I' (1514) and read it as a self-portrait in disguise: the brooding winged figure sits among the tools of geometry and craftsmanship, and the magic square in the corner is Dürer's own design, with his date, 1514, in its bottom row. Then look at the 1500 self-portrait — the Christ-like frontal pose, the fur collar — and read the audacity: a 28-year-old comparing himself to the savior was unprecedented.

name: El Greco
teaser: El Greco — 'the Greek,' born Domenikos Theotokopoulos in Crete — trained as an icon painter, moved through Venice and Rome, and settled in Toledo, Spain, where he painted figures stretched into flame and color detached from realism. His work was forgotten for 300 years and then rediscovered as proto-modern by painters who saw themselves in him.

exploreAction.targetName: El Greco — 'View of Toledo' (c. 1599) and the 'Burial of the Count of Orgaz'
exploreAction.instruction: Look at 'View of Toledo' (c. 1599) and notice what's impossible about it: the sky is storm-laden, the city is rearranged to fit the composition, and the green hills glow — a landscape painted from imagination and memory, centuries before that was allowed. Then look at the 'Burial of the Count of Orgaz' (1586) and find the split: heaven above, earth below, and El Greco's own son standing in the crowd as a witness.

name: Judith Leyster
teaser: Leyster was the first woman admitted to the painters' guild of Haarlem — in 1633, at 24 — and one of the few women of the Dutch Golden Age with a documented independent career. Her work was then misattributed to Frans Hals for nearly two centuries, until her monogram — a star, a pun on her surname meaning 'lodestar' — was discovered on the canvas.

exploreAction.targetName: Judith Leyster — 'The Proposition' (1631) and the Hals misattribution
exploreAction.instruction: Look at 'The Proposition' (1631) and read the scene carefully: a woman sewing, a man leaning over her offering coins — the painting is a warning about solicitation, and the candle and the woman's focused face tell you the moral. Then read the attribution story: 'The Carousing Couple' was hung as a Frans Hals until the 1890s, when Leyster's star monogram was found.

name: Angelica Kauffman
teaser: Kauffman was one of only two female founding members of London's Royal Academy in 1768 — the other being Mary Moser — and one of the most celebrated painters in Europe in her lifetime, a favorite of Goethe. She painted history and myth in the neoclassical manner, and her fame was so complete that her name appeared in the memoirs of her age's greatest men.

exploreAction.targetName: Angelica Kauffman — 'Zeuxis Choosing Models' (c. 1778)
exploreAction.instruction: Look at 'Zeuxis Choosing Models for His Painting of Helen of Troy' (c. 1778) and notice the feminist argument hidden in the neoclassical surface: Kauffman, a woman, paints the ancient story of a male artist choosing a model — and her composition makes the women the subject, not the selection.

name: J.M.W. Turner
teaser: Turner — 'the painter of light' — made the sky itself the subject of painting, dissolving ships, storms, and trains into atmosphere decades before Impressionism. He was so famous in his lifetime that he could exhibit paintings with no titles (the catalog simply said 'the picture of a ship in a storm'), and he left 300 paintings and 19,000 watercolors to the nation.

exploreAction.targetName: J.M.W. Turner — 'Rain, Steam and Speed' (1844) and 'The Fighting Temeraire'
exploreAction.instruction: Look at 'Rain, Steam and Speed' (1844) and find the hare — a tiny animal running across the railway tracks, Turner's symbol of the old world fleeing the new train. Then read the audacity of 'The Fighting Temeraire' (1839): the heroic warship of Trafalgar is being towed to the scrapyard by a dirty little tug, and Turner, who painted it from memory, knew exactly what the image said. The Temeraire was voted Britain's favorite painting in 2005.

name: Eugène Delacroix
teaser: Delacroix's Liberty Leading the People (1830) — Liberty as a bare-breasted woman with a rifle and a flag, stepping over the barricades — has been the image of revolution for two centuries, reproduced in everything from Coldplay albums to French stamps. It was painted in three months after the July 1830 uprising, and the Louvre displayed it behind glass for decades because of repeated vandalism.

exploreAction.targetName: Eugène Delacroix — 'Liberty Leading the People' (1830)
exploreAction.instruction: Look at Liberty Leading the People and notice who's in the crowd: the worker with the saber, the student with the pistol, the child with the pistols — and the top hat of the bourgeois on the left, who is there to remind you which class won. Then read the painting's politics: Delacroix painted it as propaganda for the July Monarchy, and the regime hung it, then hid it, as its own politics changed.

name: Jean-François Millet
teaser: Millet made the peasant the hero of French painting: The Gleaners (1857) shows three women bending to collect leftover grain in the fields, a subject his critics called dangerous and socialist. He was part of the Barbizon school, and his quiet scenes of rural labor influenced van Gogh, who copied him constantly.

exploreAction.targetName: Jean-François Millet — 'The Gleaners' (1857) and van Gogh's copies
exploreAction.instruction: Look at The Gleaners and notice the horizon line: the three women are in the foreground, but the abundant harvest behind them — the haystacks, the loaded cart — tells you the gleaners work at the very bottom of the economy. Then read the painting's reception: it was exhibited in 1857 to reviews accusing Millet of 'sowing the seeds of revolution,' which tells you how political a painting of field work could be.

name: Rosa Bonheur
teaser: Bonheur was the most famous woman painter of the 19th century — The Horse Fair (1855), her monumental study of horses at the Paris horse market, toured Europe and America, and Queen Victoria received her. To study animals at slaughterhouses and markets, she got a police permit to wear men's clothing, and she was the first woman awarded the French Legion of Honor.

exploreAction.targetName: Rosa Bonheur — 'The Horse Fair' (1855)
exploreAction.instruction: Look at The Horse Fair and notice the anatomy: Bonheur studied horses at the Paris horse market for 18 months, making endless sketches, and the painting's power comes from that research — the rearing, shoving, muscular realism has no sentimental gloss. Then read her working methods: she kept a menagerie of animals at home, painted from dissections, and treated her career with an ambition that shocked and thrilled her era.

name: Edgar Degas
teaser: Degas painted dancers — some 1,500 works of ballerinas — with the eye of a scientist and the angles of a photographer, though he always denied being an Impressionist. He also made the only sculpture exhibited in his lifetime, the Little Dancer of Fourteen Years, which shocked Paris with its real tutu and real hair.

exploreAction.targetName: Edgar Degas — 'The Dance Class' (1874) and 'Little Dancer of Fourteen Years'
exploreAction.instruction: Look at 'The Dance Class' (1874) and notice the composition's strangeness: the dancers are off-balance, cut off by the frame, and arranged diagonally — Degas was obsessed with the accidental-looking moment. Then look at the Little Dancer (1881) and read its reception: the critics called her a 'rat' and a 'flower of the gutter,' and the sculpture was hidden away for 40 years.

name: Georges Seurat
teaser: Seurat built A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte (1886) from millions of tiny dots of pure color — pointillism — a technique he called divisionism, based on optical theory. It took two years, and when it was exhibited it made him the leader of the avant-garde at 27; he died at 31, leaving the movement he founded to others.

exploreAction.targetName: Georges Seurat — 'A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte' (1886)
exploreAction.instruction: Look at La Grande Jatte from across the room, then walk close: the picture reassembles from dots into solid figures — the dog, the monkey, the woman with the parasol. Then read the theory: Seurat placed complementary colors side by side so the eye, not the paint, would mix them — the same principle behind television pixels. The figures are frozen and posed, and art historians still argue whether the island's Sunday crowd is a satire or a dream.

name: Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec
teaser: Toulouse-Lautrec — aristocrat, dwarf, chronicler of Montmartre's nightlife — painted and drew the dancers and drinkers of the Moulin Rouge in posters that invented modern graphic design. His legs stopped growing after two childhood falls; he made his short stature the vantage point from which he saw everything.

exploreAction.targetName: Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec — 'At the Moulin Rouge' (1892) and the La Goulue poster
exploreAction.instruction: Look at 'At the Moulin Rouge' (1892) and find the figures Lautrec painted repeatedly: the dancers, the absinthe drinkers, and the painter himself at the back, small and peripheral. Then look at his poster of La Goulue (1891) — flat color, bold type, cropped figures — and read why it mattered: it turned the poster into an art form and made Montmartre's performers into icons. His world was loud, and his line is the sharpest in the century.

name: Egon Schiele
teaser: Schiele — Gustav Klimt's protégé — drew the human body with an intensity that got him arrested: in 1912 the police seized his drawings and he spent 24 days in prison on charges of distributing erotic images. He died in the 1918 flu pandemic at 28, having produced some 3,000 works in his final decade.

exploreAction.targetName: Egon Schiele — the twisted self-portraits and the 1912 arrest
exploreAction.instruction: Look at a Schiele self-portrait and notice what he does to the body: the limbs are twisted, the ribs and tendons drawn as if under pressure, the face gaunt — the body as confession rather than beauty. Then read the 1912 arrest: his drawings of adolescent nudes led to a trial, and the judge burned one drawing in the courtroom.

name: Kazimir Malevich
teaser: Malevich painted the most radical painting of the 20th century — Black Square (1915), a plain black square on a white ground — and declared art's 'zero of form': the end of representation. He called the movement Suprematism, and the painting's first public display hung it high in a corner, where Russians hang icons.

exploreAction.targetName: Kazimir Malevich — 'Black Square' (1915) and 'White on White' (1918)
exploreAction.instruction: Look at Black Square and then read the icon theory: Malevich hung it in the corner reserved for Orthodox icons, and its meaning is inseparable from that gesture — the square as a replacement for the divine image. Then look at 'Suprematist Composition: White on White' (1918), three years later: the square has become almost invisible, and art has nearly vanished into pure feeling.

name: René Magritte
teaser: Magritte painted pipes that are 'not a pipe,' apples that hide faces, and men in bowler hats whose heads float in clouds — the most imitated images in modern art. His 1929 painting 'The Treachery of Images,' with its famous caption 'Ceci n'est pas une pipe' ('This is not a pipe'), is the single most quoted artwork about images in existence.

exploreAction.targetName: René Magritte — 'The Treachery of Images' (1929) and 'The Son of Man'
exploreAction.instruction: Look at 'The Treachery of Images' and read the paradox slowly: the painting shows a pipe and says it isn't one — and it's right, because it's a painting of a pipe.

name: Joan Miró
teaser: Miró's paintings — stars, moons, ladders, and biomorphic shapes floating on bright fields — look childlike and are anything but: he called them 'assassinations of painting,' and they were worked and reworked over months. The ladder is his recurring symbol for escape — he used it to leave the earth and, he said, to leave the studio.

exploreAction.targetName: Joan Miró — 'The Hunter (Catalan Landscape)' (1923) and the Constellations
exploreAction.instruction: Look at 'The Hunter (Catalan Landscape)' (1923–24) and find the coded elements: the hunter's eye, the heart, the ladder, the sardine — Miró said the painting is a map of a day in the countryside. Then look at the 'Constellation' series (1940–41), made during the German occupation of France: small, jewel-like canvases of stars and arcs painted while Europe was dark, which Miró called his 'sky paintings.'

name: Tamara de Lempicka
teaser: Lempicka painted the Jazz Age's art deco icons — sleek, angular women with polished faces and cigarette holders, figures of cool glamour. She was a Polish aristocrat who fled the Russian Revolution, arrived in Paris, and made herself the painter of the era's wealth; her 1925 self-portrait in a green Bugatti is the image of modern femininity she invented for herself.

exploreAction.targetName: Tamara de Lempicka — 'Self-Portrait in a Green Bugatti' (1925)
exploreAction.instruction: Look at 'Self-Portrait in a Green Bugatti' (1925) — she never actually owned a Bugatti — and notice the angles: the scarf, the head tilt, the sharp chin all cut the canvas like facets. Then read the paradox of her career: she painted the rich and became one of the most successful women painters of the century, then was forgotten for decades and revived in the 1970s.

name: Grant Wood
teaser: Wood's American Gothic (1930) — the farmer with the pitchfork and his stern companion — is the most parodied painting in American history, and Wood intended it as a dignified portrait of rural Iowa, not a satire. He based the farmer on his dentist and the woman on his sister, who insisted the painting showed them as 'proper people.'

exploreAction.targetName: Grant Wood — 'American Gothic' (1930)
exploreAction.instruction: Look at American Gothic and notice the details that are actually Gothic: the arched window, the pitchfork echoing the overalls, the strict symmetry — Wood called it a portrait of 'the kind of people I fancied should live in that house.' Then read the reception: Iowans were furious at first, seeing caricature; the painting won a prize at the Art Institute of Chicago and became a national icon within a decade.

name: Andrew Wyeth
teaser: Wyeth painted Christina's World (1948), the second-most-famous American painting after American Gothic: a woman in a pink dress crawling through a field toward a farmhouse. The model, Christina Olson, was paralyzed from the waist down and refused a wheelchair — she crawled everywhere, which is exactly what the painting shows, though Wyeth removed the signs of struggle.

exploreAction.targetName: Andrew Wyeth — 'Christina's World' (1948)
exploreAction.instruction: Look at Christina's World and notice what Wyeth changed: Christina was 55 when he painted her; the figure is young, and the distance to the house is compressed. The painting's pull comes from that tension — dignity against the impossibility of the task.

name: Lucian Freud
teaser: Freud — grandson of Sigmund — painted the human body with an unblinking scrutiny that made him the most important figurative painter of his era: sagging skin, awkward poses, hours-long sittings. His 'Benefits Supervisor Sleeping' (1995) set the record in 2008 for the most expensive painting by a living artist ($33.6 million).

exploreAction.targetName: Lucian Freud — 'Benefits Supervisor Sleeping' (1995) and the long sittings
exploreAction.instruction: Look at a Freud portrait and read the method behind the mercilessness: he painted from life, sometimes for 16-month sittings, and his portraits record the sitter's endurance as much as their face. Then look at 'Benefits Supervisor Sleeping' — a 275-pound woman asleep on a sofa — and read the response: critics called it grotesque, and its record price made it famous.

name: Gerhard Richter
teaser: Richter is the most expensive living artist in history (an abstract sold for $46.3 million in 2015) and the rare painter who works in two opposite styles at once: photo-realist paintings blurred from photographs, and huge abstract canvases scraped with a squeegee. He has said both are attempts 'to make a picture without knowing what it is.'

exploreAction.targetName: Gerhard Richter — 'Betty' (1988) and the squeegee abstracts
exploreAction.instruction: Look at a blurred photopainting ('Betty,' 1988, is the masterpiece — his daughter seen from behind, based on a photo) and notice what the blur does: it makes a photograph into a painting, and makes memory — indistinct, emotional — the real subject. Then look at an abstract squeegee painting and read the process: Richter paints layers, then drags a long squeegee across them, letting chance destroy what he made.

name: Georg Baselitz
teaser: Baselitz turned his paintings upside down in 1969 — and has painted most of his work that way since, as a way of 'liberating the subject from content.' He is the most important German painter to grapple with the country's postwar shame, and his 1963 exhibition was closed by prosecutors for obscenity.

exploreAction.targetName: Georg Baselitz — the inverted paintings and the 1963 seizure
exploreAction.instruction: Look at an inverted Baselitz and notice the effect: once the painting is upside down, the image (a figure, an eagle, a forest) becomes paint first and subject second — which is the point he has spent 50 years making. Then read the 1963 scandal: his painting 'The Big Night Down the Drain' was seized by German prosecutors for obscenity, making him famous at 25. His upside-down bodies are an argument about what Germany could and couldn't look at.

name: Takashi Murakami
teaser: Murakami coined 'Superflat' — the aesthetic that flattens Japanese art history, anime, and consumer culture into one surface — and his smiling flowers, mushroom clouds, and skulls became the most recognizable contemporary Japanese art of the century. He also collaborated with Louis Vuitton, which made his art global in a way galleries never could.

exploreAction.targetName: Takashi Murakami — the Superflat flowers and the mushroom-cloud series
exploreAction.instruction: Look at a Murakami flower and notice what's missing: no depth, no shading, just outline and flat color — the Superflat principle, which Murakami argues is the continuation of Japanese art from ukiyo-e through anime. Then read the darker layer: the same smiling flower appears in 'The Castle of Tin Tin' and in his mushroom-cloud paintings, and he has said his work is about Japan's postwar trauma and its consumer compensation.

name: Zao Wou-Ki
teaser: Zao Wou-Ki fused Chinese calligraphy and landscape with Western abstraction — he was born in China in 1920, moved to Paris in 1948, and became one of the most successful Asian painters of the 20th century. His large abstract canvases — which he said were landscapes in his bones — sold for record prices in the 2010s, decades after his best period.

exploreAction.targetName: Zao Wou-Ki — the calligraphic abstracts (1960s) and the late canvases
exploreAction.instruction: Look at a Zao Wou-Ki abstract from the 1960s and notice the two traditions meeting: the sweeping, ink-like gestures of calligraphy and the layered oil color of European abstraction — his paintings are landscapes that don't name themselves. Then read the turning point: in 1971 he stopped painting for a year after his second wife's death, and when he returned, the work opened up into the luminous, monumental canvases that made his late reputation.

name: Helen Frankenthaler
teaser: Frankenthaler invented the 'soak-stain' technique: pouring thinned paint onto raw canvas so it soaked in like dye, eliminating the brushstroke entirely. Her 1952 painting 'Mountains and Sea' — painted when she was 23 — is considered the bridge between abstract expressionism and color field painting, and she was the movement's most influential woman.

exploreAction.targetName: Helen Frankenthaler — 'Mountains and Sea' (1952) and the soak-stain technique
exploreAction.instruction: Look at 'Mountains and Sea' (1952) and notice the consequence of the technique: there is no brushstroke, no texture, no edge — the color is inside the canvas, and the painting is as much an object as an image. Then read the history: Frankenthaler showed the soaking method to Morris Louis and Kenneth Noland, who built Color Field painting from it — she never patented the idea, and her generosity shaped a generation.

name: Joan Mitchell
teaser: Mitchell painted fierce, gestural abstractions — sweeping arcs of color that look like storms, flowers, and memory — and she was among the few women in the first rank of abstract expressionism. She left New York for the French countryside in 1967, where her paintings grew into huge, confident canvases built around remembered landscapes.

exploreAction.targetName: Joan Mitchell — the 'Sunflowers' series and the late French canvases
exploreAction.instruction: Look at a late Mitchell ('Noon' or any of the 'Sunflowers' series) and notice the scale and confidence: the canvases are bigger than a person, and the strokes have the sweep of weather. Then read the turning point: Mitchell, like her friend Frankenthaler, was initially overlooked by the critics who canonized her male peers, and her late recognition was part of the 1970s revision of the movement's history.

name: Faith Ringgold
teaser: Ringgold made story quilts — painted narratives stitched into fabric borders — that fuse her African American family history, feminism, and political art into a form no one else was using. Her first quilt, 'Who's Afraid of Aunt Jemima?' (1983), was a direct answer to the mammy figure, and her best-known work, 'Tar Beach' (1988), was turned into a children's book.

exploreAction.targetName: Faith Ringgold — 'Tar Beach' (1988) and the story-quilt form
exploreAction.instruction: Look at 'Tar Beach Part I' (1988) and read the story in the fabric: the girl Cassie flies over the George Washington Bridge, claiming the sky — and the quilt's borders carry text narrating her flight, so the art is read as much as seen. Then read the form's history: Ringgold began quilting with her mother, a fashion designer, and turned the craft into a vehicle for stories about Black life that painting alone couldn't carry.

name: Howardena Pindell
teaser: Pindell is best known for her 'video drawings' — canvases covered in thousands of small punched-out circles, many backed with paper dots — and for 'Free, White and 21' (1980), a 12-minute video in which she performs her experiences of racism against a white actress dismissing them. She has been unflinching about both aesthetics and politics since the 1960s.

exploreAction.targetName: Howardena Pindell — the video drawings and 'Free, White and 21' (1980)
exploreAction.instruction: Look at a 'video drawing' up close and then from a distance: the punched dots read as pure pattern from across the room and as an obsessive, physical labor when you're near — Pindell has said the repetitive process is part of the meaning. Then watch 'Free, White and 21': Pindell, in a blonde wig and whiteface, plays the dismissive white woman while her real voice narrates experiences of discrimination.

name: Kerry James Marshall
teaser: Marshall paints Black life at monumental scale — interiors, gardens, housing projects, portraits — in a style that mixes realism with flat, graphic color, and he has said his project is to make Black figures so present in painting that they can't be ignored. His work sells for tens of millions, and he is widely considered the most important living American painter.

exploreAction.targetName: Kerry James Marshall — the 'Garden Project' and the Black-pantheon portraits
exploreAction.instruction: Look at 'Vignette (The Joy of Living)' or the 'Garden Project' series and notice the two directions: real spaces (the housing project, the garden) and impossible ones (the same spaces transformed into paradise). Then read his stated ambition: he has said he wants to create images of Black life with 'the authority of a master' — European painting's language used for subjects it never admitted.

name: Amy Sherald
teaser: Sherald paints Black Americans in flat, gray-scale skin against saturated backgrounds — most famously her 2018 official portrait of Michelle Obama, which made her the first Black woman to paint a First Lady's portrait. The gray skin is her signature: she has said it 'removes the color from the conversation' and lets the viewer see the person.

exploreAction.targetName: Amy Sherald — the Michelle Obama portrait (2018) and the gray-skin portraits
exploreAction.instruction: Look at the Michelle Obama portrait and notice what Sherald kept and removed: the First Lady sits in a geometric dress by a Black designer, against a patterned background — and her skin is flat gray, which shocked the public and was exactly the point. Then read her method: she works from photographs, and the gray skin pushes the figure into a space that's neither naturalistic nor abstract.

name: Njideka Akunyili Crosby
teaser: Akunyili Crosby builds large figurative paintings from photo transfers, acrylic, charcoal, and collaged fabric — dense domestic scenes of Nigerian life that layer her two homes, Lagos and Los Angeles, into one image. Her breakthrough works show a young couple (she and her husband) in interiors where Nigerian family photographs and American pop imagery share the same wall.

exploreAction.targetName: Njideka Akunyili Crosby — 'Drown' (2012) and the domestic layers
exploreAction.instruction: Look at 'Drown' (2012) or 'The Beautiful Ones' and spend time with the surfaces: the figures are painted, but the backgrounds are built from photo transfers of Nigerian family archives and patterned fabric — the domestic details (the lacy curtains, the portraits) are as much the subject as the people.

name: Wangechi Mutu
teaser: Mutu makes collages, paintings, and sculptures that splice the female body with machine parts, plants, and animal forms — a science-fiction critique of how Black women's bodies are represented and mutilated. She grew up in Nairobi, trained in sculpture, and her work has moved from intimate collage to monumental bronze figures in public plazas.

exploreAction.targetName: Wangechi Mutu — the hybrid collages and the Rockefeller Center bronzes
exploreAction.instruction: Look at an early collage (the 'Pin Up' and 'Sleeping Serpent' series) and read the hybrid bodies: the figures combine magazine cutouts, ink, and organic forms into creatures that are beautiful and wounded at once. Then read her stated subject: the imagery of the exoticized, violated, medicalized Black female body in Western culture — and her answer, which is to build new bodies entirely.

name: Lynette Yiadom-Boakye
teaser: Yiadom-Boakye paints invented portraits of Black people who don't exist — figures made up from her imagination, titled after the times they could have lived ('The Hour of Bewilderbeast'). She has said she 'makes paintings with the people in them as props' and that she has 'no interest in realism as a process.'

exploreAction.targetName: Lynette Yiadom-Boakye — the invented portraits and 'The Hour of Bewilderbeast'
exploreAction.instruction: Look at a Yiadom-Boakye portrait and read the absence: the sitters are fictional, with no backstory, no commission, no identity — which is precisely the point she has made for two decades.

name: Jadé Fadojutimi
teaser: Fadojutimi — born in London in 1993, of Nigerian and Japanese heritage — paints huge, saturated canvases of memory and emotion: layered strokes, bold color, and gestural forms that suggest places and feelings without naming them. She is among the youngest artists ever to see her work auctioned for millions, and she has said her paintings are 'maps of my mind.'

exploreAction.targetName: Jadé Fadojutimi — the memory maps and the saturated canvases
exploreAction.instruction: Look at a Fadojutimi canvas and notice the size and the color first: the paintings swallow the wall, and the palette — electric blues, pinks, yellows — is emotional before it's pictorial. Then read her stated method: she paints from memory of places she's been (her mother's garden, a walk) and of feelings, and the canvases are built over many sessions of layering and erasing.

name: Salman Toor
teaser: Toor paints intimate, nocturnal scenes of queer South Asian life — men in bars, apartments, and hammams, rendered with loose brushwork and glowing color. Born in Lahore, he came out as gay while living in Pakistan, and his work has been read as a portrait of 'what it's like to be gay and South Asian' — a subject he has said is 'both personal and political.'

exploreAction.targetName: Salman Toor — 'The Bar' and the queer South Asian scenes
exploreAction.instruction: Look at a Toor painting ('The Bar' or 'Friends in a Green Room') and notice the light: the scenes glow from within, and the figures — men dancing, talking, watching — inhabit the space with ease that took the artist decades to find.

name: Amoako Boafo
teaser: Boafo — from Accra, Ghana — paints Black subjects, often people he knows, with bold finger-painted marks and expressive color against abstracted flat backgrounds.
